text: 1.1. Having said this much about the gnostic, by way of a rapid survey, let us now proceed to what comes next; and faith, in its turn, must be examined again. For there are those who draw a distinction, holding that our faith has to do with the Son, but knowledge with the Father. They fail to notice that, in order truly to believe in the Son, one must believe that he is the Son, that he came, and how, and for what purpose, and concerning his passion; while it is necessary also to know who the Son of God is. Now neither is knowledge without faith, nor faith without knowledge; nor again is the Father without the Son, since the very name of Father implies a Son, and the Son is the true teacher concerning the Father. And in order that one may believe in the Son, he must know the Father, to whom the Son also belongs; and again, in order that we may come to know the Father, we must believe in the Son, because it is the Son of God who teaches. For we pass from faith to knowledge, and through the Son to the Father. The knowledge of the Son and the Father, which is according to the gnostic rule that is truly gnostic, is the apprehension and grasp of truth by means of the truth. We, then, are those who are believers in what is disbelieved, and gnostics in what is unknown — that is, gnostics in what is unknown and disbelieved by all, but believed and known by the few; gnostics not in word, registering deeds, but in contemplation itself.

1.2. Blessed is he who speaks into the ears of those who hear; and faith is the ears of the soul. It is this faith that the Lord hints at when he says, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear" — that, by believing, one may understand what he says, and as he says it. Indeed Homer too, the most ancient of poets, in using "hearing" for "perceiving" — the particular for the general — writes most pointedly, "and they themselves heard it." For, taken as a whole, the concord and harmony of the faith on both sides comes to one and the same end, salvation. We have for our unerring witness the apostle, who says: "For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift, so that you may be strengthened" — that is, "that I may be encouraged together in you, through our mutual faith, both yours and mine." And again, a little further down, he adds: "For the righteousness of God is revealed in it, from faith to faith." So the apostle plainly proclaims a twofold faith — or rather one faith, admitting of growth and perfecting. For common faith lies underneath like a foundation; thus, to those who longed to be healed and were moved by faith, the Lord would say, "Your faith has saved you." But the special faith, built up upon it, is brought to perfection together with the believer, and is rounded off along with that faith which comes through learning, and through fulfilling the commandments of the Word — such as the apostles were, of whom it was said that faith can move mountains and transplant trees.

1.3. Hence, perceiving the greatness of the power, they asked that faith be added to them — that faith which, like a grain of mustard seed, bites into the soul to its profit and grows mightily within it, so that upon it may rest our reasonings about things on high. For if a man knows God by nature, as Basilides supposes — calling the special faith intelligence, and at once a kingdom, and the creation of beautiful things, and worthy of the substance of its maker, existing close to him — interpreting it as substance and not as a thing in his own power, as nature and as hypostasis, the boundless beauty of an undeferred creation, and not as the rational assent of a soul that has freedom of will, then the commandments, both those of the old covenant and those of the new, are superfluous, since one is saved by nature, as Valentinus would have it, and is by nature faithful and elect, as Basilides thinks. In that case nature would have been able, at some time or other, even without the Saviour's coming, to shine out of itself. But if they say that the Lord's sojourn was necessary, then the special properties of nature have departed from them, since election is saved by learning and purification and the doing of good works, and not by nature. For Abraham, who believed by hearing the voice that under the oak in Mamre promised, "To you I give this land, and to your seed" — was he elect or not? If he was not, how did he believe at once, as it were by nature? But if he was elect, their hypothesis is undone, since election is found even before the Lord's coming, and is indeed saved; for "it was reckoned to him for righteousness."

1.4. If anyone, daring to follow Marcion, should say that the Creator saves the man who believes in him with a salvation proper to himself, the power of the Good will be outdone by it, coming late and after the Creator they so applaud, and itself only then setting about to save, either by teaching or by imitation of the other. But even if the Good thus saves, according to them, he does so neither over his own creatures nor with the consent of him who made the creation, but by force or by guile. And how is he still good, who is thus and is later? But if his place differs, and the abode of the Almighty falls short of the abode of the Good God, still the will of him who saves does not fall short of the Good, since it was that which made the beginning. Foolish, then, are the unbelievers, as is shown from what we have already gone through; for "their paths are crooked, and they do not know peace," says the prophet. "Foolish and unlearned questionings avoid," the inspired Paul exhorted, "because they breed quarrels." And Aeschylus has cried out: "Do not toil in vain at things that bring no profit."

1.5. For we know that the inquiry which proceeds together with faith, building upon the foundation of faith the magnificent knowledge of the truth, is the best of all. We know, too, that what is plain is not inquired into (as whether it is day, when it is day), nor what is obscure and will never become plain (as whether the stars are even or odd in number), nor again what admits of opposite arguments — and those things admit of them which can be argued with equal force by those who handle the contrary position, as whether the unborn child is a living being or not. There is a fourth kind, when from one of these two sides an irrefutable and indissoluble argument is put forward. If, then, the ground for inquiry is removed in every one of these ways, faith is made firm; for we set before them that irrefutable proposition, namely that it is God who speaks, and who, concerning each one of the matters I am investigating, supplies the answer in Scripture.

1.6. Who, then, is so godless as to disbelieve God, and to demand of God proofs as one demands them of men? Again, of inquiries, some require sense-perception — as if one asks whether fire is hot or snow white; some require admonition and rebuke, as Aristotle says, like that question, whether one ought to honour one's parents. And there are some that deserve punishment, such as demanding proofs whether there is providence. Providence, then, existing, it is impious to hold that the whole work of prophecy and of the dispensation concerning the Saviour did not come about according to providence; and perhaps one ought not even to attempt to prove such things, since the divine providence is manifest both from the sight of all visible things, which are works of skill and wisdom — some of them coming to be in order, others manifested in order — and from the fact that he who gave us being and life gave us also reason, wishing us to live rationally and well. For the Word of the Father of all is not this uttered word, but the wisdom and most manifest goodness of God, and again a power all-mastering and truly divine, not incomprehensible even to those who do not confess him — an all-sovereign will.

1.7. But since some are unbelievers and some contentious, not all attain to the perfection of the Good. For neither is it possible to attain it without choice, nor again does the whole rest upon our own resolve — as, for instance, the outcome. For by grace we are saved — yet not without good works, but we must, being by nature disposed toward the Good, acquire a certain zeal for it; and we must possess a sound resolve, unrepenting in the pursuit of what is noble, for which above all we have need of the divine grace, of right teaching, of pure docility, and of the drawing of the Father toward himself. For, being bound to this earthly body, we apprehend the things of sense through the body, but lay hold of the things of mind through the rational faculty itself. And if anyone expects to grasp all things by sense, he has fallen far from the truth. Spiritually, then, the apostle writes concerning the knowledge of God: "For now we see as through a mirror, but then face to face." For to few is the vision of the truth given. So Plato too says in the Epinomis: "I do not say it is possible for all men to become blessed and happy, except a few — as long, that is, as we live; this I lay down. But there is a good hope that, when one has died, he may attain all things." The same is the purport of the words in Moses: "No one shall see my face and live." For it is plain that no one can, during the time of this life, grasp God clearly; but "the pure in heart shall see God," when they have come to the final perfection. For since the soul was too weak to apprehend the things that are, we had need of a divine teacher. The Saviour is sent down, both teacher and supplier of the acquisition of the Good, the holy token of the great and unutterable providence.

1.8. "Where, then, is the scribe? Where is the disputer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?" he says. And again: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will bring to nothing" — meaning, plainly, these would-be wise men and these contentious ones. Beautifully, then, does Jeremiah say: "Thus says the Lord: Stand upon the ways and ask for the everlasting paths, which is the good way, and walk in it, and you shall find purification for your souls." "Ask," he says, and learn from those who know, without contentiousness and without strife. And having learned the way of truth, let us walk it straight, without turning back, until we light upon what we long for. With reason, then, did the king of the Romans — Numa was his name — being a Pythagorean, first of all men found a temple to Faith and Peace. And to Abraham, who believed, righteousness was reckoned. He, while pursuing the lofty philosophy of things in the air, and the sublime study of the motions of the heavens, was called Abram, which is interpreted "lofty father"; but afterwards, when he looked up to heaven — whether he saw the Son in the Spirit, as some explain it, or a glorious angel, or in some other way came to know a God greater than the creation and than all the order within it — he takes on the alpha, the knowledge of the one and only God, and is called Abraham, having become, instead of a natural philosopher, wise and a lover of God. For it is interpreted "elect father of sound." For the audible word resounds; and the father of this is the mind, and the mind of the earnest man is what is chosen out.

1.9. And I am moved very greatly to praise the poet of Acragas, who sings the praises of faith in some such fashion as this: "O friends, I know indeed that truth is in the words I shall declare; but very grievous it is to men, and the onset of faith upon the mind is full of envy." For this reason the apostle too exhorts us, that our faith may be "not in the wisdom of men" — of those who profess to persuade — "but in the power of God," which alone, even without demonstrations, by bare faith, is able to save. "The most approved knows how to guard against what is merely believed; and moreover justice will lay hold of the framers and witnesses of falsehoods," says the Ephesian. For he too, having learned from the barbarian philosophy, knows of the purification by fire of those who have lived ill — which the Stoics afterwards called conflagration; in accordance with which they teach that the individual man will rise again, thus paying court to the resurrection. Plato says that the earth is at certain times purified by fire and water, somewhat thus: "Many and various destructions of men have come to pass, and will come to pass — the greatest by fire and water, and others, lesser, by countless other means." And a little after he adds: "But the truth is, there is a shifting of the bodies that move about the earth and through the heavens, and at long intervals there comes a destruction of things upon the earth by a great fire." Then concerning the deluge he goes on: "But when, in turn, the gods purge the earth with waters and flood it, the herdsmen and shepherds in the mountains are preserved, while those in the cities among us are swept by the rivers into the sea.

1.10. We have shown, in the first book of the Stromateis, that the philosophers of the Greeks are called thieves, as having taken the most authoritative of their doctrines from Moses and the prophets without acknowledgement. To these things we shall add this also: that those angels who had obtained the lot above, slipping down into pleasures, told out the secrets to the women — as much of them as had come to their knowledge — while the other angels concealed them, or rather kept them for the Lord's coming. From that source flowed the teaching of providence, and the revelation of things on high. And when prophecy had already been spread abroad among the poets of the Greeks, the dogmatic treatment of the philosophers came into being — in part true, when they fell upon the truth by conjecture, in part going astray, when they failed to understand what was hidden in the prophetic allegory. This it is our purpose to mark out briefly as we run through the more pressing matters.

1.11. We say, then, that faith must go forward not idle and alone, but together with inquiry. For I do not say this, that one should not inquire at all; for "Seek, and you shall find," he says. "What is sought is to be caught, but what is neglected slips away," according to Sophocles. And Menander the comic poet says the like: "All things that are sought, the wisest say, have need of care." But one must stretch out the discerning part of the soul toward the discovery, and clear away the obstacles, and cast away utterly contentiousness and envy, and strife itself, that worst of things, which shall most miserably perish from among men. For most beautifully does Timon of Phlius write: "Strife, the bane of mortals, goes about with empty din, sister and handmaid of man-slaying Quarrel; and blind she rolls about over all things, and then fixes herself upon a mortal's head and casts him down from hope." Then, a little further on, he adds: "Who set these to fight in deadly strife? The rabble that runs in the train of Echo; for, angered at their silence, it stirred up against men a chattering disease." And many perished over the argument that denies falsely, and the horned argument, and the hidden one, and the crocodile, and the sorites, and the veiled one, and over ambiguities and sophisms.

1.12. But to inquire about God, if it tends not to strife but to discovery, is salutary. For it is written in David: "The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him; their heart shall live for ever and ever." For those who seek according to the true seeking, praising the Lord, shall be filled with the gift that comes from God — that is, with knowledge — and their soul shall live; for the soul is allegorized as the heart that supplies the life, since through the Son the Father is made known. Yet we must not give over our ears unreservedly to all who speak and write, since cups too, when taken hold of by many by the handles and so befouled, lose their handles, and, falling besides, are themselves broken. In the same way those who have befouled the pure hearing of the faith with many trivialities, becoming at last deaf to the truth, prove useless and fall to the ground.

1.13. Not without reason, then, do we bid little children, taken hold of by the ears, to kiss their relatives — hinting, surely, by this, that the fellow-feeling of love comes to birth through hearing. And God is love, who is known to those who love, as God is faithful, who is delivered to the faithful through learning. And we must make ourselves at home with him through the divine love, that we may behold like with like, hearkening to the word of truth guilelessly and purely, after the manner of children obedient to us. And this is what was hinted at by whoever it was that inscribed over the entrance of the temple at Epidaurus: "Pure must he be who goes within the fragrant shrine; and purity is to think holy thoughts." "Unless you become as these little children," he says, "you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." For here is the temple of God, founded upon three foundations — faith, hope, and love.

2.14. We have set down sufficient testimonies, then, from the writings of the Greeks concerning faith. But that we may not wander on at excessive length, ambitious to gather together very much also concerning hope and love, it is enough to say only this: that in the Crito Socrates, setting living well and dying above mere living, thinks he has some hope of another life after his end. For in the Phaedrus, too, saying that the soul, becoming by itself alone, is able to share in true wisdom, a wisdom higher than human power, when the love of this world has given it wings toward heaven, he says that, coming through philosophic love to the goal of hope, it receives the beginning of another, everlasting life.

2.15. And in the Symposium he says that there is mingled in all a natural love for the begetting of like to like — in men, of men only; in the earnest man, of his counterpart. But it is impossible for the earnest man to do this, unless he has the virtues in perfection, by which he will instruct the young who come to him, and, as he says in the Theaetetus, will beget and bring forth men. For some are pregnant in body, some in soul; since among the barbarian philosophers too, to instruct and to enlighten is called regenerating. "And I begot you in Christ Jesus," the good apostle says somewhere. Empedocles reckons love also among the first principles, conceiving a certain combining affection: "this do you behold with the mind, and sit not amazed with the eyes." And Parmenides too, in his poem, hinting at hope, speaks thus: "Yet behold things absent as firmly present to the mind; for you shall not cut off what is from clinging to what is, neither scattering itself wholly in every way throughout the world, nor drawing together."

3.16. For he who hopes, like him who believes, sees with the mind the things of mind and the things to come. If, then, we say that something is just, and say also that something is beautiful, and speak too of a truth, yet have never beheld any such thing with the eyes but only with the mind — and the Word of God says, "I am the truth" — then the Word is to be contemplated by the mind. "And whom do you call the true philosophers?" he asked. "Those," said I, "who love the contemplation of the truth." And in the Phaedrus Plato, speaking of truth as an idea, will make it plain . . . And the idea is a thought of God, which the barbarians have called the Word of God. The words run thus: "We must dare to speak the truth, especially when speaking about truth; for the substance that is truly existent, colourless and shapeless and intangible, is to be seen by the pilot of the soul, the mind, alone." And the Word, coming forth, became the cause of creation; and afterwards he begets even himself, when the Word became flesh, that he might also be seen. The just man, then, will seek the discovery that comes of love, and, hastening toward it, is happy; for "to him who knocks," he says, "it shall be opened. Ask, and it shall be given you." For those who take the kingdom by violence are said to force their way, not by contentious arguments, but by the perseverance of a right life and by unceasing prayers, wiping out the stains of their former sins. "And one may choose evil in crowds. But for him who toils, God also lends a hand. For not in the midst do the unconquerable gifts of the Muses lie, for the chance comer to bear away."

3.17. The recognition of one's own ignorance, then, is the first lesson for him who walks according to reason. Being ignorant, a man sought; and seeking, he finds the teacher; and finding him, he believed; and believing, he hoped; and loving, he is thenceforth made like to the beloved, striving to be that which he first came to love. Such a method Socrates points out to Alcibiades, who asks thus: "Do you not think I could know about the just in any other way?" "Yes, if you should find it out." "But do you not hold that I could find it out?" "Most certainly, if you should seek it." "Then do you not think I would seek it?" "I do, if you should think you did not know." In this way too the lamps of the prudent virgins, lit by night in the great darkness of ignorance — which night the Scripture hinted at — are the prudent souls, pure as virgins, who, perceiving themselves set in worldly ignorance, kindle the light and rouse the mind and illumine the darkness and drive out ignorance and seek the truth and await the appearing of the teacher. "A multitude of philosophers," said I, "is impossible." "Many are the bearers of the wand, but few are the bacchants," according to Plato; for "many are called, but few chosen." And "not in all," says the apostle, "is knowledge." "And pray that we may be delivered from absurd and wicked men; for faith is not for all." And the philosophic poetry of Cleanthes the Stoic writes the like, somewhat thus: "Look not to opinion, wishing to become wise on a sudden, nor fear the undiscerning and shameless opinion of the many. For the multitude has no understanding judgement, whether of just things or of noble; only among few men shall you find it."

3.18. More sententiously the comic poet says, in brief: "It is shameful to judge of noble things by the loud din." For they have heard, I think, that beautiful Wisdom that says to us: "In the midst of the witless, watch your opportunity; but in the midst of the thoughtful, persevere." And again: "The wise will hide knowledge." For the many demand demonstration as a pledge of the truth, not content with the salvation that comes by bare faith. "But to evil men it is altogether natural to disbelieve those who hold sway over the truth; but as our Muse bids you to give pledges, learn, now that the argument has been cloven within your inward parts." For to evil men it is habitual, says Empedocles, to wish to master the truth through disbelieving it. But that our things are reputable and worthy of belief, the Greeks shall come to know as the argument is more closely examined in what follows; for by the like we are taught the like. "Answer," says Solomon, "the fool out of his folly." Therefore to those who ask after their own kind of wisdom we must hold out what is proper to them, so that as easily as may be, through what is their own, they may with good reason arrive at faith in the truth. For "to all I became all things," he says, "that I might gain all"; since the rain of the divine grace too is sent down upon just and unjust. "Or is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also, if indeed God is one," cries the noble apostle.

4.19. But since they are not willing to believe, with right reason, either in the Good or in knowledge unto salvation, we ourselves, reckoning their own things to be ours — because all things are God's, and especially since what is noble came to the Greeks from us — set our hand to them as they are by nature able to hear. For the great mob does not judge what is intelligent, or what is just, out of the truth, but out of whatever pleases it. And it would be pleased by none more than by those like itself. For so much of a man as is still blind and deaf, having no understanding, nor the undaunted and keen-sighted vision of a soul that loves to behold — which the Saviour alone implants — must, like one uninitiated at the rites or unmusical in the dance, being not yet pure nor worthy of the holy truth, but discordant and disorderly and material, stand still outside the divine choir; "for we compare spiritual things with spiritual." For this reason, indeed, the manner of concealment, being truly divine and most necessary to us on account of the holy Word that lies stored away in the sanctuary of truth, was hinted at by the Egyptians through what they call their inner shrines, and by the Hebrews through the veil; through which it was permitted to enter only to those who were consecrated — that is, to those dedicated to God, who had circumcised the desires of their passions through love toward the divine alone. For Plato too agreed that it is not lawful for the impure to touch the pure.

4.20. Hence the prophecies and the oracles are spoken through riddles, and the rites are not shown to all who come unreservedly, but with certain purifications and forewarnings: "For the Muse was not yet greedy of gain in those days, nor a hireling; nor were sweet, honey-voiced songs, soft of utterance, sold by Terpsichore with silvered faces." Take, for instance, those who are educated among the Egyptians: first of all they learn the method of the Egyptian letters called epistolographic; second, the hieratic, which the sacred scribes use; and last and finally the hieroglyphic, of which one kind, by means of the primary elements, is literal, and the other symbolic. Of the symbolic, one kind is literal by imitation, another is written as it were figuratively, and another is downright allegorical by means of certain riddles. Thus, wishing to write "sun," they make a circle, and "moon" a crescent shape, according to the literal kind. But figuratively, transferring and shifting things according to affinity, and altering some and reshaping others in manifold ways, they engrave them.

4.21. Thus the praises of their kings they hand down in myths treated as theology, and inscribe by means of reliefs. Of the third kind, according to riddles, let this be a specimen: the other stars, on account of their oblique course, they likened to the bodies of serpents, but the sun to that of the beetle, since it moulds a round shape out of ox-dung and rolls it facing it. And they say that this creature lives six months under the earth, and the other part of the year above the earth, and that it sows its seed into the ball and brings forth young, and that no female beetle comes into being. All those, then, so to speak, who have treated of theology, both barbarians and Greeks, hid away the first principles of things, and handed down the truth in riddles and symbols, and again in allegories and metaphors and such-like devices — like the oracles among the Greeks; and the very Pythian Apollo is called Loxias, "the oblique."

4.22. Yes, and the apophthegms of those called among the Greeks the wise men show forth, in a few words, the unfolding of a greater matter — such as, doubtless, "Spare time": either because life is short, and one ought not to spend this time in vain; or, in the opposite sense, "Spare expense" in private outlay, so that, even if you live many years, the necessaries of life may not fail you.

4.23. In the same way "Know yourself" points to many things: both that you are mortal, and that you were born a man; and further, in comparison with the other excellences of life, that you are of no account — calling oneself glorious, or rich, or, on the contrary, that, though rich and glorious, you pride yourself on no abiding advantage. And "Know for what you came into being," he says, "and whose image you are, and what is your substance, and what your fashioning, and what your kinship with the divine," and the like. The Spirit says too, through Isaiah the prophet, "I will give you treasures dark and hidden." And the treasures of God, and the wealth that does not fail, is wisdom hard to track down.

4.24. But the poets too, taught their theology by these prophets, philosophize much by way of hidden meaning — I mean Orpheus, Linus, Musaeus, Homer, and Hesiod, and those who are wise in this way. The persuasive charm of their poetry is to them a veil before the many. Dreams and symbols are all the more obscure to men, not out of envy — for it is not lawful to think of God as subject to passion — but in order that inquiry, slipping in toward the meaning of the riddles, may run up to the discovery of the truth. Thus Sophocles, the poet of tragedy, says somewhere: "And I know God to be such as this: ever to the wise a propounder of oracles in riddles, but to the dull a poor teacher, and that in few words" — using "poor" for "simple."

4.25. Plainly, at any rate, concerning all our Scripture it is written in the Psalms that it is spoken as in a parable: "Hear, my people, my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter problems from of old." And the noble apostle says the like, somewhat thus: "We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age that come to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which God foreordained before the ages unto our glory, which none of the rulers of this age has known; for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." The philosophers, indeed, were not empowered to outrage the Lord's coming; it remains, then, that the apostle is rebuking the conceit of the wise among the Jews. Therefore he adds: "But we preach, as it is written," he says, "things which eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for those who love him. For to us God has revealed them through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God." For he knows the spiritual man, the gnostic, to be the disciple of the Holy Spirit supplied by God, which is the mind of Christ. "But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit; for to him they are foolishness."

4.26. Thus the apostle, to set the common faith over against gnostic perfection, calls it in one place a foundation, in another milk, writing in this fashion: "Brethren, I could not speak to you as to spiritual men, but as to fleshly, as to babes in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able. But neither even now are you able, for you are still fleshly. For where there is among you jealousy and strife, are you not fleshly, and walking after the manner of men?" The objects of choice belong to the sinful among men; but those who have abstained from these set their minds on the things of God and partake of gnostic food. "According to the grace," he says, "given to me, as a wise master-builder I have laid a foundation, but another builds upon it gold and silver and precious stones." These are gnostic structures upon the base of faith in Jesus Christ; but stubble are the additions of the heresies, and wood and hay. "Of what sort each man's work is, the fire shall test." The gnostic edifice he hints at also in the Epistle to the Romans, saying: "For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift, to the end that you may be strengthened." But it was not possible to write of such gifts openly.

5.27. Take, for instance, the Pythagorean symbols, which hang very closely upon the barbarian philosophy in a hidden way. The Samian, then, counsels not to keep a swallow in the house — that is, not to receive a chattering, whispering, ready-tongued man, who cannot keep within him the things he is given a share in. "For the swallow and the turtle-dove, the sparrows of the field, have known the seasons of their comings," says the Scripture; and one ought never to dwell together with idle talk. Indeed the turtle-dove, murmuring, showing forth the thankless slander of reproach, is with reason expelled the house: "so do not sit by me and mutter, one from this side, one from that." But the swallow, by which the myth of the son of Pandion is hinted at, is worth abominating because of the sufferings noised abroad concerning her, of which we have received that Tereus partly suffered and partly wrought. And it pursues the musical cicadas; whence he who is a pursuer of the Word is rightly thrust away. "Yes, by Olympus-watching, sceptred Hera, I have a faithful storehouse upon my tongue," says the poetry. And Aeschylus: "I too have a key, a guard upon my tongue." Again, Pythagoras enjoined, when the pot was lifted from the fire, not to leave behind the imprint in the ashes, but to confound it; and to disturb and stir up the bedclothes upon rising from sleep. For he was hinting that one ought not only to make conceit vanish, but to leave behind not even a trace of anger — that, when it has boiled up and ceased, it should settle, and wipe out all remembrance of wrong. "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath," says the Scripture; and he who said "You shall not covet" took away all remembrance of wrong; for anger is found to be an impulse of desire in a gentle soul, set above all upon defence, irrationally.

5.28. In the same way too the bed is bidden to be disturbed, so that one may no longer keep in mind any nocturnal emission, nor any sleep by day, nor even the pleasure of the night. And perhaps he was also hinting that the murky imagination must be confounded by the light of the truth: "Be angry, and sin not," David says, teaching that one ought not to give assent to the impression, nor to bring on the deed that ratifies the wrath. Again, "Do not sail on land" is a Pythagorean symbol, and it shows that the taxes and the like, the wages of hire, being troublesome and unstable, ought to be declined. For this reason, indeed, the Word says that the tax-gatherers are hardly saved. Again, Pythagoras enjoins not to wear a ring, nor to engrave on it images of the gods — just as Moses long before plainly laid down in law that one must make no carved or molten or moulded or painted statue and likeness, that we may not cleave to things of sense, but pass over to the things of mind. For the familiarity that comes of having the sight ready to hand cheapens the majesty of the divine; and to worship the intelligible substance through matter is to dishonour it through sense. Hence the wisest of the Egyptian priests set apart the seat of Athena unroofed and open to the sky, as the Hebrews founded the temple without an image. And there are some who, worshipping God, make a likeness of the heaven that encompasses the stars, and bow down to it.

5.29. Indeed, since the Scripture says, "Let us make man after our image and likeness," I think it worth while to set down also the saying of Eurytus the Pythagorean, which runs thus. In his work On Fortune, having said that the Creator made man using himself as a pattern, he goes on: "And the body is like the rest, as being come of the same matter, but wrought by the best of craftsmen, who fashioned it using himself as an archetype." And, in a word, Pythagoras and his followers, together with Plato above the rest of the philosophers, had very close converse with the Lawgiver, as one may gather from their very doctrines. And, by some happy hitting of a divining utterance, not without God they fell together upon certain prophetic words; and grasping the truth in parts and kinds, they honoured it with names not without light, nor going outside the showing-forth of the things — having taken an impression of their kinship with the truth. Whence the Greek philosophy is like the gleam from a wick, which men kindle, stealing the light skilfully from the sun; but when the Word was proclaimed, all that holy light shone forth. Then in the houses the stolen fire is of use by night; but by day the fire is outshone, and all the night is lit up by so great a sun of the intelligible light.

5.30. Take, for instance, how Pythagoras has made an epitome of what was said by Moses concerning righteousness, saying "Do not step over the yoke-beam" — that is, do not go beyond what is equal in the distributions, honouring the justice that ever binds friends to friends, cities to cities, allies to allies; for "the equal is by nature lawful among men, but the lesser is ever set in enmity to the greater, and begins the day of hatred," as the poetry gracefully has it. For this reason the Lord says, "Take up my yoke," because it is kindly and without weight. And to the disciples who quarrelled about precedence he enjoins equality with simplicity, saying that they must become as the little children. In the same way the apostle too writes that in Christ there is no slave or free, no Greek or Jew; for the creation in Christ is new, free from contention and from greed, and is a just equality. For envy stands outside the divine choir, and jealousy and grief — wherefore the initiates also forbid eating the heart, teaching that one ought never, by heavy moods and griefs over things that befall against our will, to bite and devour the soul. Wretched, then, is that man whom Homer too speaks of as wandering alone, "devouring his own heart."

5.31. Again, since the Gospel and the apostles, like all the prophets, set down two ways, and call the one — that which is hedged about by commandments and prohibitions — narrow and straitened, and the opposite one, which leads to destruction, broad and wide, unhindered by pleasures and by passion; and since they say, "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners"; the myth of Prodicus of Ceos concerning Virtue and Vice comes forward in like manner, and Pythagoras does not shrink from forbidding men to walk the public roads, enjoining that one ought not to follow the opinions of the many, which are undiscerning and inconsistent. And Aristocritus, in the first book of his Replies to Heracleodorus, mentions a certain letter that runs thus: "Atoeas, king of the Scythians, to the people of the Byzantines: Do not harm my revenues, lest my mares drink your water." For the barbarian was symbolically signifying the war that was about to be brought upon them. In like manner too the poet Euphorion brings in Nestor saying: "And we had not yet watered our Achaean mares at the Simoeis." For this reason, indeed, the Egyptians set up sphinxes before their temples, as showing that the discourse about God is full of riddles and obscure — and perhaps also that one ought both to love and to fear the divine: to love it as gentle and kindly toward the holy, but to fear it as inexorably just toward the unholy. For the sphinx hints at the image of a beast and a man together.

6.32. It would be a long task to go through all the prophetic and legal sayings that are spoken in riddles, picking them out one by one; for nearly the whole Scripture utters its oracles in some such way. It is enough, I think, for one who has understanding, by way of demonstration of what is set before us, that a few examples be put forward. Take, for instance, how the concealment is owned by the reference, recorded among the Hebrews, of the seven enclosures about the ancient temple, and by the arrangement of the high priest's robe reaching to the feet, which through its varied symbols related to things visible hints at the whole framework that stretches from heaven to earth. And the covering and the veil were variegated with hyacinth and purple and scarlet and fine linen, hinting that the nature of the elements holds the revelation of God: for the purple is from water, the fine linen from earth, the hyacinth is likened to the air, being dusky, as the scarlet to the fire.

6.33. And between the covering and the veil, where the priests were permitted to enter, lay the altar of incense, a symbol of the earth set in the middle of this world, from which come up the exhalations. And that place was midway between the inner part within the veil, where it was permitted to the high priest alone to enter on stated days, and the outer enclosing court, open to all the Hebrews. Therefore they say it is the very midmost of heaven and earth; while others say it is a symbol of the intelligible and the sensible world. The covering, then — a hindrance to the unbelief of the laity — was stretched before the five pillars, keeping back those in the enclosure. Thus, most mystically, five loaves are broken by the Saviour and multiplied for the multitude of the hearers. For great is the number of those who cleave to the things of sense as though these alone existed. "Look round about, and take heed," says Plato, "lest one of the uninitiated overhear." And these are they who think that nothing else exists except what they can lay firm hold of with both hands, but who do not admit actions and processes of becoming and everything invisible as having a share in being; for such are they who cleave to the pentad of the senses alone. But the apprehension of God is not to be trodden by the ears, nor by those of like kind.

6.34. Hence the Son is called the face of the Father, having become the bearer of flesh through the pentad of the senses — the Word who is the announcer of the Father's distinctive being. "And if we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. We walk by faith, not by sight," the good apostle says. Within the covering, then, the priestly ministry was hidden, and it keeps off from those within it many that are without. Again, the veil of the way into the holy of holies — there four pillars stood, a token of the holy tetrad of the old covenants. And the mystic name of four letters was set upon those to whom alone the inner sanctuary was to be trodden; it is pronounced Iaoue, which is interpreted, "he who is and who shall be." And indeed among the Greeks too the name "God" contains a tetrad of letters. And into the intelligible world the Lord alone, having become high priest, enters, slipping in through the sufferings to the knowledge of the unspeakable, withdrawing above every name that is made known by the voice. Indeed the lamp-stand too lay on the south side of the altar of incense, by which were shown the motions of the seven light-bearers that make their circuits to the south. For three branches grow from each side of the lamp-stand, and upon them the lamps; since the sun too, like the lamp-stand, set in the midst of the other planets, gives of its light to those above it and to those below it, according to a kind of divine music.

6.35. The golden lamp-stand has yet another riddle, of the sign of Christ — not by its shape alone, but also by its casting light in manifold ways and in many parts upon those who believe in him and hope and look toward him through the ministry of the first-created. And they say that the seven eyes of the Lord are the seven spirits resting upon the rod that flowers from the root of Jesse. And on the north side of the altar of incense the table had its place, on which lay the setting-out of the loaves, because the things of the north are the most nourishing of the spirits. And there might be certain abodes of churches breathing together into one body and one assembly. And the things recorded upon the holy ark signify the things of the intelligible world, hidden away and shut off from the many. Indeed, those golden figures too, each of them six-winged, whether they show forth the two Bears, as some would have it, or rather the two hemispheres — and the name Cherubim means "much knowledge" — but both together have twelve wings, and by the zodiacal circle and the time that is borne along it they show forth the world of sense.

6.36. Concerning these things, I think, tragedy too, philosophizing on nature, says: "Unwearying Time goes round, full with ever-flowing stream, begetting itself; and the twin Bears, with the swift-wheeling rushings of their wings, keep watch over the Atlantean pole." And Atlas, the pole that does not suffer, may be the fixed sphere, but better perhaps it is to be understood as the unmoved age. But I think it better that the ark, called by the Hebrew name thēbōtha, signifies something else; it is interpreted "one in place of all places." Whether, then, the Ogdoad and the intelligible world is signified, or the God who comprehends all things, shapeless and invisible, let it be set aside to say now; except that it indicates rest in the company of the glorifying spirits, which are hinted at by the Cherubim. For he who had charged that not even a carved idol be fashioned would never himself have figured a statue of holy things; nor is there at all in heaven any such composite and sensible living creature. But the face is a symbol of the rational soul, and the wings are the lofty ministries and operations of the powers on the right and on the left together, and the voice is the thankful glory in unceasing contemplation.

6.37. Let it be enough to have carried the mystic interpretation thus far. The high priest's robe reaching to the feet is a symbol of the sensible world: of the seven planets, the five stones and the two carbuncles, for Cronos and the Moon. For the one is southern and moist and earthy and heavy, the other is airy; whence Artemis is called by some "the air-cleaver," being a kind of being, and the air is dusky. And the powers set over the planets, which co-operate in the generation of things here according to the divine providence, he with reason represents as set upon the breast and the shoulders, through which the generation-producing action, the first hebdomad, comes about; and the breast is the dwelling-place of the heart and the soul. And in another way too the variegated stones might be modes of salvation, set, some among the higher, some among the lower parts of the whole body that is being saved. And the three hundred and sixty bells hung from the robe are the year's time, "the acceptable year of the Lord," proclaiming and announcing the greatest appearing of the Saviour. And the golden plate, lifted up, signifies the kingly authority of the Lord, since the Saviour is the head of the church.

6.38. The plate above the head, then, is a sign of a most commanding rule; for we have heard, as it is said, that "the head of Christ is God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." Indeed the breast-piece is made up of the shoulder-piece, which is a symbol of work, and of the oracle-pouch — and this hints at the Word — and it is an image of heaven, which came to be by the Word, lying beneath the head of all things, Christ, and moving in the same way and after the same fashion. The shining emerald stones, then, upon the shoulder-piece signify the sun and the moon, the fellow-workers of nature. And the shoulder, I think, is the beginning of the hand. And the twelve set in four rows upon the breast describe for us the zodiacal circle according to the four turns of the year. And it was fitting, besides, that the law and the prophets should be set beneath the Lord's head, through which the righteous of both covenants are shown forth; for in saying that the apostles are both prophets and righteous men we should speak well, since one and the same Holy Spirit works through all. And as the Lord is above the whole world — or rather beyond the intelligible world — so too the name written upon the plate was held worthy to be above every rule and authority; and it is written by reason of the written commandments and of the sensible presence. And it is called the name of God, since, as the Son beholds the goodness of the Father, he works, being called God the Saviour, the beginning of all things, which was figured first, before the ages, from the invisible God, and has stamped all things that came to be after it.

6.39. Indeed the oracle-pouch signifies the prophecy that cries aloud and proclaims by the Word, and the judgement that is to come; since it is the same Word that prophesies and that at once judges and distinguishes each thing. And they say that the garment, the robe reaching to the feet, prophesies the dispensation according to the flesh, by which he was more nearly seen in the world. Thus the high priest, having put off the consecrated tunic — for the world, and the creation in the world, has been consecrated by him who agreed that the things made were good — bathes and puts on the other tunic, a holy of holy, so to speak, which goes in with him into the inner sanctuary; showing forth, as I think, the Levite and the gnostic, as ruler over the other priests, those others having been washed with water and clothed with faith alone and awaiting their own abode, while he himself has distinguished the things of mind from the things of sense, and, by an ascent above the other priests, hastens to the passage into the intelligible, being washed of the things here no longer with water, as before he was purified when he was being enrolled into the Levitical tribe, but now by the gnostic Word.

6.40. Pure, then, in all his heart, having ordered his whole conduct most excellently to the highest, having grown beyond the priest to something greater, downright purified both in word and in life, having put over himself the brightness of glory, having received the unspeakable inheritance of that spiritual and perfect man — which eye has not seen and ear has not heard and which has not entered into the heart of man — having become a son and a friend, he is now filled, face to face, with the insatiable contemplation. There is nothing like hearkening to the Word himself, who gives the mind more by means of the Scripture. For it says thus: "And he shall put off the linen robe, which he had put on when he entered into the holy place, and shall leave it there. And he shall bathe his body with water in a holy place, and shall put on his robe." In another way, I think, the Lord puts off and puts on, coming down into sense; in another way he who has believed through him puts off and puts on over himself, as the apostle also showed, the consecrated robe. Hence, after the image of the Lord, the most approved of the consecrated tribe were chosen as high priests, and those elected to kingship and to prophecy were anointed.

7.41. Hence the Egyptians too did not commit their mysteries to the chance comer, nor carry out the knowledge of divine things to the profane, but only to those who were about to advance to the throne, and to those of the priests judged to be most approved, by reason of their nurture and education and birth. Like the Hebrew riddles, then, in their concealment are those of the Egyptians too. Some of the Egyptians show the sun upon a ship, others upon a crocodile. And they signify that the sun, making its course through the sweet and moist air, begets time, which is hinted at by the crocodile by reason of some other priestly story. Indeed, in Diospolis of Egypt, upon what is called the sacred portal, there is figured a child, a symbol of coming into being, and an old man, of decay, and a hawk, of God, and a fish, of hatred, and again, by another signification, a crocodile, of shamelessness.

7.42. The whole symbol, then, when put together, appears to declare this: "O you who are born and pass away, God hates shamelessness." And the makers, fashioning ears and eyes out of costly material, consecrate them to the gods, dedicating them in the temples — hinting, surely, that God sees and hears all things. Besides this, the lion is to them a symbol of strength and might; just as the ox, surely, of earth itself and of husbandry and of food, and the horse of courage and boldness, and again the sphinx of might together with understanding, having the whole body of a lion, but the face of a man. In like manner to these, hinting at understanding and memory and power and skill, man is engraved by them upon the sacred things.

7.43. And further, in what are called among them the processions of the gods, they carry round golden figures — two dogs, one hawk, and one ibis — and the four figures of the statues they call four letters. The dogs, then, are symbols of the two hemispheres, as it were going round and keeping watch; the hawk, of the sun, for it is fiery and destructive — thus they ascribe pestilential diseases to the sun; the ibis, of the moon, the dark parts likened to the black, the bright to the white, of its feathers. And there are some who hold that the tropics are signified by the dogs, which guard and keep the door of the sun's passage to the south and to the north; while the hawk shows forth the equator, which is high and scorched, just as the ibis the ecliptic. For the ibis seems above the other creatures to have furnished the Egyptians with the beginning of the conception of number and measure, as the oblique circle did of the circles.

8.44. But indeed not only the most reasoning of the Egyptians, but also, besides, those of the other barbarians who reached after philosophy, were zealous for the symbolic kind. They say, for instance, that Idanthura, the king of the Scythians, as Pherecydes of Syros records, when Darius had crossed the Ister and was threatening war, sent him, instead of a letter, a symbol — a mouse, a frog, a bird, an arrow, a plough. And when there was, as was likely, perplexity over these things, Orontopagas the captain of a thousand said they would surrender the rule, conjecturing from the mouse the dwellings, from the frog the waters, from the bird the air, from the arrow the arms, and from the plough the land. But Xiphodres interpreted it the opposite way; for he said: "Unless we fly up like birds, or burrow into the earth like mice, or dive under water like frogs, we shall not escape their arrows; for we are not masters of the country." And they say that Anacharsis the Scythian, while asleep, used to hold his private parts with his left hand and his mouth with his right, hinting that one ought to master both, but that it is a greater thing to master the tongue than pleasure.

8.45. And why should I linger over the barbarians, when I may set forth the Greeks themselves as having very much used concealment? Androcydes the Pythagorean, then, says that what are called the Ephesian letters — much-talked-of among many — have the rank of symbols, and that Askion signifies darkness, since this has no shadow; Kataskion light, since it lights up the shadow; Lix is earth, by an ancient appellation, and Tetrax the year, by reason of the seasons; and Damnameneus the sun, the subduer; and Aisia the true voice. The symbol, then, signifies that divine things are set in order — as darkness to light, and the sun to the year, and the earth to the begetting of every kind of nature. And Dionysius the Thracian, the grammarian, in his work On Indication, speaks thus, word for word, concerning the symbol of the wheels: "Some signified their acts not by speech alone, but also by symbols — by speech as in the Delphic precepts, 'Nothing too much' and 'Know yourself' and the like; by symbols as the wheel that is turned in the precincts of the gods, drawn from the Egyptians, and the giving of branches to those who worship." For Orpheus the Thracian says: "Of branches, as many works as men upon earth have a care for, none has one single lot in mind, but all wheel round about; and to stand still in one part is not lawful, but each one keeps, as he began, an equal share of the course." The branches, then, are a symbol either of the first food, or that the many may come to know that the fruits flower and grow throughout, abiding very long, while they themselves have obtained but a short span of life; for this reason they will have the branches given; and perhaps also that they may come to know that, as these are burned, so they too must quickly leave this life and become the work of fire.

8.46. Most useful, then, is the kind of symbolic interpretation, helping toward many things, and toward right theology, and toward piety, and toward the showing of understanding, and toward the practice of brevity, and toward the display of wisdom; "for it is the part of a wise man," says Didymus the grammarian, "to use the symbolic mode of speech with dexterity, and to recognize what is shown forth by it." Indeed the elementary teaching of children embraces the interpretation of the four elements. For the Phrygians call water bedy, as Orpheus too: "and bedy, the bright water of the nymphs, is poured down." But the priest Dion likewise appears to write: "And taking bedy, pour it over your hands and turn to the inspection of the sacrifice." On the other hand, Philyllius the comic poet knows bedy as the air, the giver of life, by these words: "I pray to draw in the saving bedy" — which is the greatest part of health, to draw in the air pure, not befouled.

8.47. In agreement with this opinion is Neanthes of Cyzicus also, when he writes that the priests of the Macedonians, in their prayers, call upon bedy to be gracious to them and to their children — which they interpret as air. And as for zaps, "fire," some have taken it, in their ignorance, from zesis, "boiling"; but the sea is called by this name, as Euphorion in his replies to Theodoridas: "And zaps, the destroyer of ships, works mischief upon the reefs." And Dionysius the Iambic likewise: "the briny zaps groans around the raging sea." So too Cratinus the younger, the comic poet: "the zaps casts forth shrimps and little fishes." And Simmias of Rhodes: "the briny zaps was mother of the Ignetes and the Telchines." And chthon is the earth, poured out into magnitude. And plēktron, "the striker," some take as the pole, others as the air that strikes and moves all things into nature and growth, or that which fills all things.

8.48. But these men had not read Cleanthes the philosopher, who downright calls the sun the striker; for in its risings, driving home its rays as it were striking the world, it leads the light into its harmonious course; and from the sun it gives sign also to the other stars. And the sphinx is not the binding-together of all things and the revolution of the world according to the poet Aratus, but perhaps it might be the pervading spiritual tension that holds the world together; though it is better to take it as the aether that holds and binds all things, as Empedocles too says: "But come, I will tell you first the sun, the beginning, from which were made plain all the things now beheld — earth, and the much-billowing sea, and the moist air, the Titan, and the aether that binds tight all things round in a circle." And Apollodorus of Cercyra says that these verses were uttered aloud by Branchus the seer, when he was cleansing the Milesians from a plague. For sprinkling the multitude with branches of laurel, he led off the hymn somewhat thus: "Sing, O children, of the Far-worker and the Far-worker's maid"; and the people, so to speak, struck up in answer: "bedy, zaps, chthōm, plēktron, sphinx; knaxzbich, thyptes, phlegmo, drōps." Callimachus too mentions the story in his Iambics. And knaxzbich is, by derivation, the disease, from knaiein, "to grate," and "to destroy," and thypsai, "to burn with lightning." Thespis, however, the tragedian, says that something else is signified by these, writing somewhat thus: "Lo, I pour you a libation of knaxzbich, white, pressed from the dugs of yellow goats; lo, for you thyptēs, cheese mingled with red honey, I set upon your holy altars, O horned Pan; lo, for you I pour Bromius' phlegmo." He hints, I think, at the first milky food of the soul that comes from the four-and-twenty elements; after which is the food now curdled into cheese, and last the blood of the vine of the Word, the fiery wine, which teaches the gladness that perfects the discipline. And drōps is the active Word, which from the first catechizing brings the man to growth, to the measure of his stature, kindling and enlightening the man.

8.49. But there is borne about also a third copy-line for boys: "Grasp, sphinx, thief, gratingly." It signifies, I think, by the management of the elements and of the world, that the way must lie for us toward the knowledge of the more perfect, since eternal salvation is won by force and toil. For "to grasp" is to apprehend; the sphinx is the harmony of the world; "gratingly" shows forth the difficulty; and "thief" shows at once the knowledge of the Lord that escapes notice, and the day. And again — does not Epigenes, in his work On the Poetry of Orpheus, setting forth the peculiar usages in Orpheus, say that "crook-fashioned shuttles" signify ploughs, and "warp-threads" the furrows; that the "thread" is allegorized as the seed, and "the tears of Zeus" show the rain; that the Fates, again, are the phases of the moon, the thirtieth, the fifteenth, and the new moon — wherefore Orpheus calls them "white-robed," being parts of the light? And again, "the flowery one" is the spring by reason of nature, "the shining one" is the night by reason of its rest, and "the Gorgon" is the moon by reason of the face in it; and "Aphrodite" is the season in which one ought to sow — these are said in the theologian.

8.50. Such things the Pythagoreans too hinted at, allegorizing the dogs of Persephone as the planets, and the sea as the tear of Cronos. And we should find ten thousand things upon ten thousand spoken in riddles by both philosophers and poets, seeing that whole books too show forth the hidden purpose of the writer — such as the book of Heraclitus On Nature, who for this very reason was surnamed "the Obscure." Like this book is the theology of Pherecydes of Syros. For the poet Euphorion, and the Causes of Callimachus, and the Alexandra of Lycophron, and such-like works, are set as an exercise in exegesis for the boys of the grammarians.

8.51. It is not unlikely, then, that the barbarian philosophy too, of which it is our purpose to speak, should in some places prophesy in a hidden way and through symbols, as has been shown. Such, for instance, are the things Moses enjoins — these common ones: "You shall not eat the swine, nor the eagle, nor the hawk, nor the raven." For the swine signifies the pleasure-loving and unclean desire for foods, and the lickerish craving for venery, and a defiled wantonness, ever itching, material and lying in the mire, fattened for slaughter and destruction. On the contrary, he permits the eating of what parts the hoof and chews the cud, signifying, says Barnabas, that one ought to cleave to those who fear the Lord, and to those who meditate in their heart on the distinction of the word which they have received, to those who speak the ordinances of the Lord and keep them, to those who know that meditation is a work of gladness, and who chew the cud upon the word of the Lord. And what is the parting of the hoof? That the just man both walks in this world and awaits the holy age. Then he goes on: "See how well Moses laid down the law. But how could they understand or grasp these things? But we, understanding the commandments rightly, speak as the Lord willed. For this reason he circumcised our ears and our hearts, that we might understand these things."

8.52. Indeed, when he says, "You shall not eat the eagle, the hawk, the kite, and the raven," he means: "You shall not cleave to, nor be made like, those men who do not know how to provide themselves food by toil and sweat, but live by plunder and lawlessness." For the eagle signifies plunder, the hawk injustice, and the raven greed. And it is written: "With the innocent man you shall be innocent, and with the elect you shall be elect, and with the perverse you shall be perverse." It is fitting, then, to cleave to the holy, because those who cleave to them shall be sanctified. Hence Theognis writes: "From the good you shall learn good things; but if you mingle with the evil, you shall lose even the mind you have." And again, when it says in the song, "He has been gloriously glorified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea," the many-limbed, brutish, impulsive passion — desire — together with the rider mounted upon it, the charioteer who has given the reins to pleasures, he has cast into the sea, hurling them into the disorders of the world.

8.53. So too Plato, in his treatise On the Soul, says that the charioteer and the horse that has revolted — the irrational part, which is cleft in two, into spirit and desire — fall down. By which the myth too hints that Phaethon fell through the unruliness of the colts. Indeed in the case of Joseph also: his brothers, in envy of him as a youth who saw further in the matter of knowledge, stripped off his many-coloured tunic, and taking him, cast him into a pit; and the pit was empty, it had no water. Spurning the varied knowledge of the earnest man that comes of love of learning, or using only the bare faith that is according to the law, they cast it into the pit empty of water, to sell it off into Egypt, the desert of the divine Word. And the pit is empty of knowledge, into which the man cast and stripped of his knowledge — the wise man who had escaped notice — seemed to his brothers like to themselves, naked of knowledge. By another signification the many-coloured garment might be desire, leading away into a yawning pit. "And if anyone open a pit, or hew one out," it says, "and do not cover it, and a calf or an ass fall in there, the owner of the pit shall pay money and give it to his neighbour; but the dead beast shall be his."

8.54. Here bring to my aid that prophecy: "The ox knew its owner, and the ass the manger of its master; but Israel did not know me." That none of these, then, falling into the knowledge taught by you, having become a hearer of the truth, may misunderstand and stumble, "Be safe," it says, "concerning the use of the word"; and toward those who come to it irrationally, shut up the living spring that lies in the deep, but hold out drink to those who thirst for the truth. Concealing yourself, then, from those who are not able to receive the depth of knowledge, cover the pit. The owner of the pit, then — the gnostic himself — will be punished, it says, undergoing the charge of him who is offended or swallowed up by the greatness of the word, while still small-minded, or of having moved the labourer over to contemplation and set him aside, by reason of his ill-prepared faith. And he shall give money, rendering account and answer to the all-sovereign will.

8.55. This, then, is the type of the law and the prophets up to John. But he — although he spoke more plainly, as no longer prophesying but already pointing to him who was symbolically announced from the beginning as now present — nevertheless says, "I am not worthy to loose the strap of the Lord's sandal." For he confesses that he is not worthy to baptize so great a power; for those who purify must loose the soul from the body and from its sins, as one looses the foot from the bond. And perhaps too he means the last operation of the Saviour toward us, the nearest one, that which comes through his presence, hidden under the riddle of prophecy; for he who by his own showing pointed out him who was prophesied of, who announced the presence as having come, that had journeyed from afar into manifestation, truly loosed the end of the oracles of the dispensation, uncovering the meaning of the symbols. And among the Romans the things done over wills have their order — those scales and asses and acts of redemption and the touchings of the ears that are done for justice' sake — some that they may be done justly, some for the apportioning of the honour, and one that the bystander, as though some weight were laid upon him, may stand and hear and take the rank of a witness.

9.56. But, as it seems, in my zeal for demonstration I have unawares digressed beyond what is needful. For life will fail me as I set forth the multitude of those who philosophized in symbols. For the sake, then, of memory, and of brevity, and of being stretched out toward the truth, such are the writings of the barbarian philosophy. For they will have the truly true philosophy and the true theology belong only to those who have often drawn near to these writings and have given proof in faith and in their whole life. Indeed, they will have us in need of some interpreter and guide; for thus, they reckoned, the worthy would the more give themselves to study and be benefited, and would not be deceived, receiving the teaching from those who well know. And besides, all things that show through some veil display the truth as greater and more august — as fruits gleaming through water, and forms through veils which lend them certain added showings. For things in full glare both prove deceptive and let only what is plain be perceived in a single way.

9.57. It is possible, then, to take many connected meanings, as indeed we do take them, from things said with concealment. And, this being so, the inexperienced and unlearned man goes astray, but the gnostic apprehends. For this very reason they did not wish all things to be set forth nakedly to the chance comer, nor the goods of wisdom to be made common to those who have not even in a dream had their soul cleansed; for it is not lawful to hold out to all comers the things won with so great toils, nor to declare the mysteries of the Word to the profane. They say, for instance, that Hipparchus the Pythagorean, being charged with having written down the doctrines of Pythagoras plainly, was cast out of the school, and a pillar was set up over him as over one dead. Hence in the barbarian philosophy too they call dead those who have fallen away from the doctrines and have subjected the mind to the passions of the soul. "For what fellowship has righteousness with lawlessness," according to the divine apostle, "or what communion has light with darkness? And what concord has Christ with Belial, or what part has a believer with an unbeliever?" For apart are the honours of the Olympians and of the dead. "Therefore come out from among them and be separate," says the Lord, "and touch no unclean thing; and I will receive you, and I will be a Father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters."

9.58. It was not the Pythagoreans, then, and Plato alone who hid most of their teaching; the Epicureans too say that there are certain secret things even of his, and that they do not permit all to come upon these writings. And the Stoics too say that certain things were written by Zeno the first, which they do not readily permit the disciples to read, unless they have first given proof whether they philosophize genuinely. And the Aristotelians say that of his writings some are esoteric, and some common and exoteric. And those who established the mysteries, being philosophers, buried their own doctrines in myths, so that they should not be plain to all. If, then, these men, hiding away human opinions, kept the unlearned from coming upon them, was it not the more fitting that the truly holy and blessed contemplation of the things that really are should be concealed from everyone? Yet neither the things of the barbarian philosophy, nor the Pythagorean myths, nor even those in Plato — of Er the son of Armenius in the Republic, of Aeacus and Rhadamanthus in the Gorgias, of Tartarus in the Phaedo, of Prometheus and Epimetheus in the Protagoras, and besides these the myth of the war of the men of Atlantis and the Athenians in the Atlanticus — are to be allegorized outright in every name, but only so much of them as is significant of the general thought; and these things, indeed, we should find indicated through symbols under the veil of allegory.

9.59. Indeed the assembly of Pythagoras too, and his twofold fellowship with his hearers — calling the many "auditors," and certain others, who genuinely laid hold of philosophy, "mathematicians" — hinted that some things are to be spoken and some kept hidden from the many. And perhaps that twofold division of the Peripatetics too, called in their discourses the "probable" and the "scientific," is not free of a distinguishing of opinion from good repute and truth: "Let not the flower of glorious honour from mortals force you to take it up, on condition of speaking beyond what is holy." The Ionian Muses, at any rate, plainly say that the many and the seeming-wise "follow the singers of the people, and use the customs, knowing that many are bad, but few good; while the best pursue glory." For "the best choose one thing in place of all," it says, "everlasting glory among mortals; but the many are glutted like cattle," measuring happiness by the belly and the privy parts and the basest of the things within us. And the Eleatic Parmenides the great brings in a teaching of two ways, writing somewhat thus: "Both the unshaken heart of well-persuasive Truth, and the opinions of mortals, in which is no true faith."

10.60. With reason, then, the inspired apostle says: "By revelation was made known to me the mystery, as I wrote before in few words, by which, when you read, you may understand my insight into the mystery of Christ, which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets." For there is a certain learning of the perfect, concerning which, writing to the Colossians, he says: "We do not cease to pray for you and to ask, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, to walk worthily of the Lord unto all pleasing, bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God, being strengthened with all power according to the might of his glory." And again: "according to the dispensation of God given to me," he says, "toward you, to fulfil the word of God, the mystery which has been hidden from the ages and from the generations, but now has been made manifest to his saints, to whom God willed to make known what is the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles."

10.61. So that there are, on the one hand, the mysteries hidden until the apostles, and delivered by them as they received them from the Lord — hidden in the old covenant — which have now been made manifest to the saints; and, on the other hand, "the riches of the glory of the mystery among the Gentiles," which is faith and hope toward Christ, whom elsewhere he has called a foundation. And again, as it were ambitious to make knowledge plain, he writes somewhat thus: "Admonishing every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ." Not every man simply, since then there would be no unbeliever; nor again every believer perfect in Christ, but he says "every man," meaning, so to speak, the whole man, purified in body and in soul. For, that knowledge is not for all, he plainly adds: "knit together in love, and unto all the riches of the full assurance of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery of God in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving." And the thanksgiving is made not for the soul only and for spiritual goods, but also for the body and for the goods of the body.

10.62. And still more plainly he uncovers that knowledge is not for all, adding: "Praying at the same time for us also, that God may open to us a door of utterance, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which also I am bound, that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak." For there were certain things delivered without writing. To the Hebrews, for instance, he says: "And though you ought to be teachers by reason of the time" — that is, as having grown old in the old covenant — "you have need again that someone teach you what are the elements of the beginning of the oracles of God, and you have become such as have need of milk and not of solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk is unacquainted with the word of righteousness, for he is a babe, entrusted with the first lessons; but solid food is for the perfect, for those who through habit have their senses exercised to discern good and evil. Therefore, leaving the word of the beginning of Christ, let us press on toward perfection."

10.63. But Barnabas too, who himself co-proclaimed the word with the apostle in the ministry to the Gentiles, says: "I write to you more simply, that you may understand." Then, a little later, already setting down a trace of the gnostic tradition more plainly, he says: "What says the other prophet, Moses, to them? 'Behold, thus says the Lord God: Enter into the good land which the Lord swore to give — the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob — and inherit it, a land flowing with milk and honey.' What does knowledge say? Learn. Hope, it says, upon him who is about to be made manifest to you in the flesh, Jesus; for a man is earth that suffers, since out of the face of the earth was the moulding of Adam. What then does it mean, 'into the good land, a land flowing with milk and honey'? Blessed be our Lord, brethren, who has set wisdom and understanding of his hidden things in us. For the prophet says, 'Who shall understand a parable of the Lord, except the wise and understanding man, and he who loves his Lord?'" — since it is given to few to contain these things. For "not out of envy," he says, "did the Lord proclaim, in a certain Gospel, 'My mystery is for me and for the sons of my house'" — making his election in safety and without anxiety, that the household of those he has chosen, having received what is proper to them, may become superior to envy. For he who has no knowledge of good is evil, since there is one good, the Father; and to be ignorant of the Father is death, as to know him is eternal life, by participation in the power of the incorruptible. And not to be corrupted is to partake of divinity, while corruption is brought on by the falling away from the knowledge of God.

10.64. Again the prophet: "And I will give you treasures hidden, dark, unseen, that they may know that I am the Lord God." The like to these David too sings: "Behold, you have loved truth; the obscure and hidden things of your wisdom you have made plain to me." "For day to day utters speech" — that which is plainly written — "and night to night declares knowledge" — that which is hidden mystically; "and there are no words nor speeches whose voices are not heard" by God, who said, "Shall a man do anything in secret, and I shall not see him?" For this reason discipleship has been called enlightenment, as making plain the hidden things, when the teacher alone uncovers the lid of the ark — contrary to what the poets say of Zeus, that he laid hold of the jar of goods but opened the jar of ills. "I know that, coming to you," the apostle says, "I shall come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ" — calling the spiritual gift and the gnostic tradition, which, present, he longs to impart to them present (for these things could not be made plain by letter), the "fullness of Christ," "according to the revelation of a mystery kept silent through eternal times, but now made manifest through the prophetic Scriptures, and, by the command of the eternal God, made known to all the Gentiles unto the obedience of faith" — that is, to those of the Gentiles who believe, that he is; but to few of these is it shown what these mysteries are.

10.65. With reason, then, Plato too, in the Letters, treating of God, says: "It must be told you in riddles, so that, if the tablet should suffer anything in the recesses of sea or land, he who reads it may not understand."
